crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Self-Driving Laboratories
children.blurb: Self-driving laboratories are experimental platforms that combine automated hardware, sensors, and machine learning to plan, execute, and interpret experiments with limited human intervention.

children.name: Digital Twins for Experiments
children.blurb: Digital twins for experiments are computational models that mirror a physical laboratory system, such as a bioreactor, spectrometer, or robotic assay line, in enough detail to predict its behavior under different conditions.

children.name: Instrument and Sensor Data
children.blurb: Instrument and sensor data in laboratory automation and simulation covers the raw and processed signals from analytical instruments, environmental sensors, imaging systems, and robotic lab equipment.

children.name: Optimising Lab Protocols
children.blurb: Optimising lab protocols uses AI and simulation to refine the sequence, timing, and parameters of experimental procedures.

children.name: Forecasting Lab Supplies
children.blurb: Forecasting lab supplies means predicting future demand for consumables, reagents, equipment parts, and other inventory in research and clinical laboratories.

sections.body: Laboratory automation and simulation is the use of software and robotic equipment to run experiments, model them before they happen, and manage the data they produce. In practice, artificial intelligence reads instrument logs, proposes the next experiment in a self-driving loop, and adjusts liquid handling or temperature settings. Machine learning also builds simplified digital twins that predict how a reaction or assay will behave under different conditions. These systems work on real tasks like choosing reagent volumes, scheduling runs, and flagging sensor readings that fall outside expected ranges.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The most reliable results come from narrow, well defined optimisation problems, such as tuning a single chemical reaction or a standard assay on one instrument. Closed loop systems can reduce the number of manual trials for those cases, but they do not generalise easily to new equipment or new protocols. Digital twins are often coarse approximations that need frequent recalibration against physical measurements. Instrument data remains messy because file formats and calibration practices differ between labs. Protocol optimisation can overfit to the specific machine it was trained on, and supply forecasting breaks down when usage patterns shift suddenly.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader can start with Self-Driving Laboratories to see how planning, execution, and learning fit into one loop. Digital Twins for Experiments then shows how a simulated version of an experiment can reduce wasted physical runs. Instrument and Sensor Data covers the raw inputs that both the twins and the optimisation models depend on. Optimising Lab Protocols explains how machine learning tunes steps like mixing times or temperatures. Forecasting Lab Supplies closes the loop by predicting what materials will be needed for upcoming work.
